newsitem.title: USA: Minn. airports commission plans $300 mln expansion.
newsitem.headline: Minn. airports commission plans $300 mln expansion.

text.p: Metropolitan Airports Commission is expected to approve next month an estimated $300 million new runway project at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport for completion by 2003, the deputy executive director of planning and environment said.
The commission's planning and environment committee has scheduled a public hearing on the expansion plan for Tuesday, Nigel Finney said.
The committee is expected to recommend approval of the plan in early August for adoption by the commission on Aug 18, he said.
Financing for the project likely will include federal grants and the issuance of debt, although specifics have not been completed, Finney said.
The commission has already started the environmental impact statement process and anticipates receiving a federal record of decision in December, Finney said.

Enough land is available for the runway itself, but more must be acquired for a protective zone to the south where development will be restricted, including land owned by the Mall of America developers, Finney said.
The commission wants to buy Metropolitan Sports Facilities Commission land near the Bloomington mall and exchange it for the Mall of America parcel, Finney said.

The 53-acre sports commission parcel has been appraised at $28.5 million, sports facilities Executive Director Bill Lester said. It had been the site of the Met Center arena, razed in the early 1990s after the Minnesota North Stars hockey franchise moved to Dallas, he said.

Some older hotels in the protective zone area will have to be removed for the new runway which also includes restrictions on residential development, stadiums and schools, airports spokesman Walt Hellman said.

The airport now has two parallel runways and one crossing runway, Hellman said. The proposed new runway would run north-south separate from the others with all takeoffs and landings to the south, he said.
Minnesota lawmakers in 1996 rejected the possibility of developing a new airport based on a study of longrange facility needs.
The new runway would resolve capacity issues until 2020 and possibly beyond, Finney said.
